sections.head: Contributions
paragraphs: We advance applied information economics research by considering capital market participants and the information asymmetries that they and company executives contend with in M&A. Unlike in other market contexts in which the theory has been deployed (e.g., used cars, hiring, etc.), M&A transactions not only involve buyers and sellers, but they also give rise to information asymmetry between buyers and capital market participants. The latter provide buyers with financial resources and have a vested interest in these transactions. However, capital market participants also face adverse selection, unless full information is given to them by company executives entering into M&A transactions. A wealth of studies has examined the implications of information asymmetry between buyers and sellers in M&A, and by considering the implications of information asymmetries for acquiring firms and capital market participants that have been neglected in previous research, we conclude that previous research has understated the implications of information frictions in M&A markets.

Our empirical analysis considers whether corporate communication in earnings calls reflects a firm's M&A activity. We also examine whether information disclosure reduces the effects of adverse selection otherwise borne by capital market participants. We build a corporate strategy dictionary and text-analyze the contents of millions of questions and answers in over 80,000 conference calls. We implement propensity-score matching algorithms to mitigate concerns surrounding sample selection and endogeneity, thereby isolating the implications of M&A activity for information disclosures to capital markets. The upshot of these analyses is that a All samples are obtained by matching firms with a high use of corporate dictionary (i.e., at or above the median) with firms with a low use of the same (i.e., below the median), using propensity score and nearest-neighbor matching techniques. The models are estimated using OLS regressions. The dependent variables in the models above represent the absolute difference between the median of the analysts' forecast of firms' earnings and their actual earnings in the quarter following the focal earnings call, divided by the median of the analyst' forecast. Standard errors and p-values appear below each parameter estimate. b The parameter estimates and corresponding standard errors are multiplied by 1,000 for legibility purposes. c These variables were logged to remedy skewness.

we find strong empirical support for our predictions. Specifically, both analysts and company executives discuss a firm's corporate strategy more when the firm is involved in M&A activity in the period of time leading up to the call. In addition, the more M&A transactions the firm has engaged in, the more the firm's corporate strategy becomes the subject of discussion during the call. Interestingly, executives often discuss corporate strategy even when not prompted to do so by analysts, yet we see far less focus on corporate strategy topics during the financial crisis. Lastly, the accuracy of analysts' earnings forecasts decreases with aggressive questioning of the firm's corporate strategy by analysts, and it increases with time devoted by executives to explaining the firm's corporate strategy.

sections.head: Research implications and future research
paragraphs: There are a number of implications and interesting follow-on research opportunities brought forth by this study. At the broadest theoretical level, information economics in strategy has become a central theoretical framework used to explain firms' corporate strategy agendas across a broad spectrum of corporate activities, such as mergers and acquisitions, but also strategic alliances, joint ventures, corporate venture capital, licensing, etc. While our focus is on M&A, there are clear opportunities to explore whether the complexity of firms' corporate strategy portfolios involving different transactions affect the quantity and quality of information flows from executives to capital market participants. This sort of investigation promises to be fruitful because the pursuit of competitive advantage through corporate strategy can be highly heterogeneous across firms.

Without a doubt, a great deal of research has gone into whether and how these diverse pursuits allow firms to outperform their peers, by creating market power, superior access to resources and markets, preemption of entry, etc. However, we know little about the relationship between the complexity of a firm's corporate strategy and the adverse selection problem affecting its stakeholders, where this problem is known to create a direct and consequential impact on the firm's ability to raise capital and compete in the first place. This paper lays preliminary foundations for this line of research, but future work along the lines we draw would be highly informative and beneficial to the advancement of knowledge in this area. For instance, future research might examine other types of corporate deals besides M&A (e.g., foreign direct investment, technology partnerships, etc.). It would also be valuable to extend this analysis to explore firms based in other countries subject to different information intermediaries and institutions that can shape both their corporate strategies and ability to obtain financial and other resources in factor markets (e.g., Ahuja and Yayavaram, 2011). We also think it would be interesting to examine equity market responses to previously announced M&A transactions leading up to the earnings calls, as well as the method of payment used to execute these deals, in order to determine whether such factors may trigger differential questioning on the topic of corporate strategy.

Remaining within the confines of M&A research, there are several promising avenues that deserve attention. First, while we distinguish firms based on whether or not they engage in M&A and based on how much they engage in M&A, there are opportunities to consider the qualitative characteristics of different M&A transactions. It is well known that M&A transactions are far from homogeneous, such that some deals bring together firms from like industries, markets, corporate cultures, etc., while others involve diversification into new products, geographies and corporate cultures, instead. Our objective in this project was to begin to establish a connection between M&A activity and corporate communication, but a more nuanced examination of the relationship into the microfeatures of M&A activity and their effects on information disclosures and adverse selection involving capital market participants would be useful. Such work could also take up agency considerations and explicitly consider other factors affecting tradeoffs in corporate communications (e.g., appropriation and competition concerns).

Research in such directions would inform us on the degree to which particular types of transactions impose information costs on firms and capital markets, and they might also have consequences on other stakeholders and markets. Given our focus on shareholders and information intermediaries in capital markets, it would also be interesting to extend our analysis to consider other stakeholders and factor markets. For instance, research might consider how executives explain the implications of their complex M&A transactions to suppliers, partners, potential employees, etc. The degree to which adverse selection concerns in M&A spill over to these stakeholders would provide a more complete picture of the information costs of M&A and the degree to which adverse selection within M&A deals is subject to externalities across stakeholder groups. Even our study might therefore be understating the consequences of these information frictions in M&A markets.

In exploring the heterogeneity of M&A and its consequences, there are also a number of opportunities to consider how the solutions firms use to address adverse selection on M&A may or may not affect capital market participants. To begin with, the negative effects of information asymmetry may be reduced if a seller credibly conveys an information signal to a buyer (Spence, 1973). Research in strategy has studied whether the presence of signals may help to lubricate corporate transactions, generally finding support for this hypothesis. For example, prior work has shown that signals issued when firms go public facilitate their subsequent acquisitions in M&A markets (Ragozzino and Reuer, 2007), or that prior alliances with prominent partners function certify the quality of entrepreneurial firms, which in turn lends them needed credibility (e.g., Sorenson and Stuart, 2001;Chang, 2004;Lee et al., 2011). To our knowledge, none of this work has examined the role of signals as a tool to reduce the effects of information asymmetry between firms and their stakeholders while the firm is engaging in corporate transactions such as M&A. For instance, the very same signals on a target's resources and prospects that help firms come together in corporate transactions may also alleviate adverse selection concerns for shareholders and allow for the well-functioning of capital markets, in particular. Our research has indicated that information costs surrounding M&A might be higher than previous research has suggested, because it has not addressed the adverse selection problems that shareholders face. By contrast, the signals that firms rely upon when carrying out M&A and other corporate transactions might also be beneficial to exchanges in other factor markets (e.g., capital markets, markets for suppliers, etc.), which suggests that their benefits might also be understated in previous research. For example, within the context of our research, it would be interesting to examine whether acquisitions in which signals are issued by a target firm result in less questioning of the transaction by analysts and in more precise earnings forecasts, as well. Therefore, we suggest that the role of signals does not stop with facilitating a corporate deal, but it potentially extends into corporate communication and the workings of capital markets. We would also note that other remedies that a firm relies upon in alleviating adverse selection in M&A (e.g., contingent payments, contractual safeguards, etc.) might not have such spillover effects on information intermediaries and capital markets, however.

Along similar lines, it would be interesting to examine whether pre-acquisition learning plays a role in corporate communication and information asymmetry between companies and their stakeholders. For example, if a company decided to integrate vertically and acquire a supplier with which it had worked for several years, then one would expect that the need to unearth information about the value-adding properties of this acquisition would be lower than if the acquisition involved an upstream firm with no prior relationship to the acquirer. Prior work has informed us of the strategic benefits of staging investments such as these, in order to reduce asymmetric information between buyers and sellers (Mitchell and Singh, 1992;Balakrishnan and Koza, 1993;Mody, 1993;Hagedoorn and Sadowski, 1999;Porrini, 2004). While such successive exchanges and sequential investment approaches might also reduce information costs of shareholders and other stakeholders, we know nothing of whether this sort of learning-based approach to M&A yields similar advantages when the relationship of interest is between company insiders and the firm's shareholders and other stakeholders.

Relatedly, our findings indicate that a larger number of analysts attending a conference call tends to reduce the amount of questioning on firms' corporate activity. While a deep dive of the reasons for this relationship lies outside the scope of this work, a potentially intriguing question that stems from this result is that the quality and quantity of information disclosure issued by firms may depend on analyst attendance. If so, some firms may "get away" with less disclosure, which may then trigger different outcomes in capital markets and in the competitive environment: On the one hand, prospective shareholders and bondholders will have less information by which to evaluate the company. On the other hand, companies will be less compelled to provide information on their corporate strategies to competitors. Investigating the relationships between analyst attendance, information disclosure and firm performance would be valuable in future research.

sections.head: Conclusion
paragraphs: In sum, this paper offers an initial attempt to bring to the fore the problem of adverse selection in corporate strategy, not as it pertains to the buyers and sellers directly involved in corporate deal making, but rather in the context of acquiring firms and their own shareholders. Despite the maturity of the M&A literature and corporate strategy field more generally, the implications of M&A and information asymmetries between firms and shareholders have been neglected. This likely reflects the greater attention given to moral hazard concerns as well as the direct, immediate application of theoretical models from information economics that do not involve shareholders as third parties directly in these transactions (e.g., a single buyer and seller in a transaction for a used car, insurance contract, etc.). However, the follow-on consequences of M&A for shareholders can have important implications for firms' abilities to raise external resources and ultimately compete in their marketplaces. Our theory and evidence therefore suggest that prior acquisition studies have understated the consequences of information frictions in M&A markets. Research along the lines we have suggested would help to connect M&A studies with other current streams of strategy research (e.g., on stakeholders, analysts, information disclosures, etc.), and we hope that our study encourages future research that better accounts for the implications of M&A for other factor markets.
